_comment: Narration for out/final2. Each cue names the BEAT it lands on, from that scene's .beats.jsonl, so the voice tracks the picture. Budgeted at Brian's MEASURED 2.9 words/sec. Claims checked against source: TLS is BearSSL so TLS is never claimed as own work; no Win32; no Wi-Fi; no visualiser (it does not visibly move); image size is the measured ~4 MB, not the manual's stale 660 KB.
_voice: Brian - Deep, Resonant and Comforting (chosen by arin 2026-08-07)

cues.text: This is UnoDOS. A complete graphical operating system, written from scratch.
It boots on an ordinary PC straight to a desktop. No install, no command line. Nineteen megabytes, half of it game data.
Everything here was built for this system: the window manager, the toolkit, the icons, the fonts. None of it is borrowed from another operating system.
Windows do not jump to their positions, they move. Drag one to an edge and it snaps there.
Hold the switcher key and the highlight slides between windows.
There are four virtual desktops, and any window can be sent to another one.
Every control here works from the keyboard as well as the pointer.
The whole interface can be re-dressed while it runs.
Ten themes ship with it, including careful takes on Mac OS 7, Windows 3.1, and the Commodore 64.
Fonts, interface scale and screen resolution all change the same way.
The wallpapers are drawn by the system rather than shipped as pictures. Nothing here needed a restart.
UnoDOS ships its own office suite: a faithful recreation of Office 97.
This is an actual Word document, opened from disk. Not an export, not a simplified copy: the fonts, the formatting and the layout all come out of the original file.
And this is a real Excel workbook. The whole suite was rebuilt from nothing, and checked against a live copy of Office 97.
Its formulas are intact and recalculating. A document written on this machine opens on a normal PC, and one written on a PC opens here.
There is a web browser, and it runs JavaScript.
This page is being laid out and scripted by the system's own engine, written for this project.
What is unusual is that the engine is switchable while the browser is running.
Same page, same browser, now running on QuickJS instead. Two independent implementations, chosen at runtime.
And this is the real web. Wikipedia, over a secure connection, fetched and parsed and laid out by this machine.
The whole article is here, navigation sidebar and all, on an operating system somebody wrote from nothing.
The player is modelled on Winamp.
This music is being decoded on the machine itself, by decoders written for this project. MP3, AAC, MIDI and WAV.
And it wears real Winamp skins. That is an original, unmodified skin file, with its ten band equaliser underneath.
The image viewer reads the formats you would expect, animated GIFs included.
This is where it gets unusual. UnoDOS carries its own development environment, and both C and Python are first class citizens in it.
This is a real C program, open on the machine that is about to compile it.
Control B compiles it, with a real sixty-four bit backend.
Control R runs it, and the application opens beside the editor. No second computer, no cross compiler, no toolchain anywhere else.
And the same editor, with the same two keystrokes, will take Python instead. Either language is a first class way to write software for this machine.
That one runs on the system's own Python runtime, and opens as an ordinary application.
Alongside Studio there is UnoCode: an editor built in the shape of Visual Studio Code, and running on this machine.
Go to File, an explorer, tabs, a minimap, syntax highlighting. All of it drawn by the operating system underneath it.
Every command has a name, and every name is in one searchable list.
That command came from an extension, and running it just executed real JavaScript, in the system's own engine.
The terminal is the editor's own. Six times seven, evaluated on the machine.
That one is a Visual Studio Code theme file, dropped in unmodified. Keybindings and snippets load the same way.
It ships its own applications, games included.
And this is Doom.
Not the original C, but a renderer written in Python, reading a real Doom game file, on the system's own Python runtime.
It walks real Doom level geometry, textured and perspective correct, on an operating system that also has to be a desktop.
A Freedoom WAD: its levels, its sounds and its music, straight off the disk.
The machine can also be automated, and Python is how you do it.
This script asks the system about itself: how much memory is free, which volumes are mounted, what the network card has sent, which windows are open.
Then it starts driving.
Those keystrokes are coming from the script. It opens the menu, walks down it, launches an application, and then asks the system what changed. The machine is operating itself.
There is an SSH client, and it is the same SSH the rest of the world uses.
Curve twenty five five one nine key exchange, an Ed25519 key, AES encryption. All of it written for this project, and tested against OpenSSH.
That is a real shell on a real Linux box across the network.
The answers are coming from that machine, not this one.
There are games, and they are the project's own. This is Dostris, with its music coming out of the machine's own sequencer.
Pac-Man, with ghosts that actually hunt you. This one runs silent: its sound was never written.
And OutLast, keeping score while the road comes at you.
The music is the machine's too. This is the built-in tracker, four channels, playing a pattern live.
The system window names the drivers it is actually using: storage, input, network, power. This machine is running on UnoDOS's own drivers, not the firmware's.
Networking is its own TCP/IP stack, written for the project.
The system log is live, and can be shipped to a logging server like any other machine on the network.
You can try this yourself, right now, in a browser.
Or write it to a USB stick and boot your own PC from it.
One system, wherever you want it.
